questions.corrige_markdown:
**The Brazzaville Conference of 1944.**

- **What it was.** A meeting of French colonial governors and officials held in **Brazzaville** (French Congo) from 30 January to 8 February 1944, called by General **Charles de Gaulle** (head of the Free French) to decide the future of France's African colonies. Governor-General Félix Éboué of French Equatorial Africa played a leading role; no African delegate took part.
- **Why.** Cameroon had rallied to the Free French in August 1940, and Africans had given soldiers and resources to the war; France needed to reward them and to prepare the post-war empire.
- **Recommendations.** The progressive end of forced labour and of the *indigenat*, the development of schools, health and the economy, wider political participation (local assemblies and African representation in the French constituent assembly), and trade unions.
- **Limits.** It rejected independence and self-government (the final declaration excluded any idea of autonomy outside the French empire), and kept the principle of French sovereignty.
- **Effects.** It led to the 1944 decree permitting trade unions, the end of forced labour (1946) and the abolition of the *indigenat*, the creation of the French Union (1946) and elected representatives for Cameroon; it also encouraged Cameroonian nationalists to demand more.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) The UPC revolts of the 1950s.

(5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**The UPC revolts of the 1950s.**

- **Origins.** The Union des Populations du Cameroun (UPC), formed in 1948 under Ruben Um Nyobè, demanded reunification and independence. The French accused it of communism and used administration pressure and electoral fraud against it (elections of 1951-52, 1956).
- **The May 1955 riots.** In May 1955 serious riots broke out in Douala, Yaounde, Mbanga and other towns after the UPC protested at the administration; many people were killed and the UPC was **banned in July 1955**.
- **Guerrilla war.** UPC leaders went into hiding or exile (Félix Moumié to Cairo, Accra and Conakry); armed groups fought in **Sanaga-Maritime (Bassa region)** under Um Nyobè and later in the **Bamileke region** (West) under Ernest Ouandié. The French army and police used harsh methods (resettlement camps, mass arrests).
- **Key events.** Um Nyobè was killed by French forces on 13 September 1958; Félix Moumié died in Geneva in November 1960 (poisoned); the fighting went on after independence until the early 1970s (Ouandie was executed in 1971).
- **Effects.** The UPC was weakened and divided, thousands died, and Ahidjo's government (with French help) took power; the demand for independence was met on terms favourable to France.
themes: upc and french repression in cameroon

questions.corrige_markdown:
**The Loi Cadre of 1956.**

- **What it was.** The *Loi Cadre* (framework law), also called the **Defferre law** after the French minister for overseas territories Gaston Defferre, was passed by the French parliament on **23 June 1956**.
- **Provisions.** It gave **universal adult suffrage** (one electoral college), set up elected territorial assemblies and governing councils, and allowed African ministers to run local affairs (health, education, agriculture), while France kept defence, foreign affairs, justice and finance.
- **Application in Cameroon.** Cameroon, a trust territory, was dealt with by a **statute of 1957** (decree of 16 April 1957) creating an elected **Legislative Assembly (ALCAM)** and a government headed by a Prime Minister (Mbida, then Ahidjo). The High Commissioner kept important powers. The elections of December 1956 were held without the banned UPC.
- **Effects.** It prepared the transition to self-government and independence, increased political activity among Cameroonians, and was meant to calm nationalism; the UPC rejected it as a way to keep French control.
themes: loi cadre reforms in french cameroon

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) The resignation of André Marie Mbida in 1958.

(5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**The resignation of André-Marie Mbida in 1958.**

- **Background.** Mbida, leader of the Démocrates Camerounais, became the first Prime Minister of Cameroon in May 1957 after the elections to ALCAM, with Ahidjo as Deputy Prime Minister.
- **Causes of his fall.** He was reproached for a hard line against the UPC (he refused an amnesty), for a pro-French and slow attitude to independence and reunification (he did not fix a date for independence), and for an authoritarian style which offended many deputies, especially the northern members of ALCAM led by Ahidjo.
- **How it happened.** In **February 1958** several ministers and deputies withdrew their support; Mbida lost his majority and resigned (about 16 February 1958); the French authorities, including the High Commissioner Pierre Messmer, are said to have preferred to work with Ahidjo.
- **Consequences.** **Ahidjo** became Prime Minister (18 February 1958), formed a new government, obtained from France the end of the trusteeship and a date for independence (1 January 1960).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(e) Trade Union activities in the 1940s.

(5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Trade Union activities in the 1940s.**

- **Legalisation.** Before 1944 African workers could not form unions. After the Brazzaville Conference, a decree of **7 August 1944** allowed trade unions in French colonies.
- **Formation.** The **Union des Syndicats Confédérés du Cameroun (USCC)** was founded in Douala in 1944, linked to the French CGT. A French teacher, **Gaston Donnat**, helped to create it and the Marxist study circles which trained young Cameroonians; **Ruben Um Nyobè** was later its leader (1947).
- **Activities.** Unions demanded higher wages, the end of forced labour, family allowances and equal pay; a strike at Douala in **September 1945** ended in clashes with police and deaths. They also trained leaders and gave workers a political voice.
- **Importance.** The unions gave birth to political parties; the USCC was behind the creation of the **UPC in 1948**. Christian unions also appeared later.
